title: Thinking and memory: how the brain builds memories, sleeps and feels
source: DeepKids Combined. A DeepKids topic beyond the boards (the parts of the brain, kinds of memory, how memory is rebuilt, attention, sleep and dreams, emotions, animal minds and consciousness), building on the senses and body chapters of NCERT, Cambridge and NIOS. No textbook needed.
summary: A memory is not a recording: the brain builds it again each time you remember. Your child maps the main parts of the brain on a paper hat. They meet Henry Molaison, who could not make new memories, and Brenda Milner, the scientist who studied him. They catch their own memory adding a word that was never read out, and find out why honest eyewitnesses can be wrong. They learn a new skill in a mirror, and look at the live debates about why we sleep and what emotions are. Last, they meet the biggest open question in science: what consciousness is.
builds_on: Class 3: neurons and synapses, nerves and reflexes, the blind spot and illusions, attention as a spotlight, the forgetting curve, memories as paths strengthened by practice and sleep, other animals' minds, and thinking without a brain. Here: the parts of the brain, kinds of memory, reconstructive memory, sleep science and its debates, emotions and consciousness. Links to 'Our closest cousins' (Class 5: do apes know themselves?) and 'Health' (Class 3: sleep and feelings).
goals: By the end your child can name the main parts of the brain and say what each mostly does, and explain that the brain changes as we learn.
By the end your child can name three kinds of memory and explain what Henry Molaison's story taught scientists.
By the end your child can show that memories are rebuilt each time, using a false-memory test, and explain why that matters for eyewitnesses and for history.
By the end your child can describe what happens in sleep and explain one live debate about why we sleep.
By the end your child can compare two scientific views of what emotions are, and discuss which animals might be conscious.
By the end your child can explain why consciousness is still an open question, and weigh more than one view of it.

words: cortex
the wrinkly outer layer of the brain, used for thinking, sensing and moving
cerebellum
the 'little brain' at the back that coordinates balance and skilled movement
brainstem
the part joining brain and spinal cord that runs breathing and heartbeat
hippocampus
a seahorse-shaped part deep in the brain needed to form new memories of events
amygdala
an almond-shaped part involved in fear, alarm and emotional memories
hemisphere
one half, left or right, of the brain
neuroplasticity
the brain's ability to change its connections as we learn
reconstructive memory
the idea that we rebuild a memory each time we recall it
consciousness
being aware: having experiences, a 'what it is like' to be you
emergence
when something new appears from many simple parts working together
panpsychism
the idea that some simple form of experience is part of everything

days.title: Your earliest memory
days.goal: Remember Class 3, find your earliest memory, and hear the story.

steps.title: Remember Class 3
steps.do: Ask: 'In Class 3, what did we find out about the brain?' Good answers: the brain is made of about 86 billion nerve cells called neurons, which pass messages across tiny gaps called synapses. Reflexes act before we decide. The blind spot shows that the brain fills in what we see. We notice what we pay attention to and miss much else, like the gorilla in the ball-passing video. We forget fastest soon after learning, and practice and sleep make memories last. Say: 'This year we find out that a memory is not a recording. The brain builds it again each time.'

steps.title: Your earliest memory
steps.do: Ask your child: 'What is the very first thing you remember?' Listen fully. Then ask: 'In that memory, are you looking out through your own eyes, or can you see yourself?' Many people see themselves from outside, which cannot be how they first saw it. Ask: 'Could some of it come from photos, or from hearing the story told?' Share your own earliest memory. Say: 'Most people remember almost nothing from before about age 3 or 4. Scientists call this childhood amnesia, and nobody fully knows why.'

steps.title: Story: What the Handycam Saw
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). Ask the story questions. Don't explain yet why both cousins were sure. Your child will test their own memory on Day 4.

steps.title: Start mirror drawing
steps.do: Start Experiment e2, mirror drawing. Set up the mirror and the book as the experiment says, and draw the double-lined stars (or draw one and photocopy it). Ask first: 'Will you get better at this? How fast?' Your child traces a star while looking only in the mirror. Do five tries today, and write down the time and the number of errors for each.

need: a mirror that can stand up
a book or card to hide the hand
15 stars with a double outline (draw them, or draw one and photocopy it)

days.title: A map of the brain
days.goal: Learn the brain's main parts, and that the brain changes.

steps.title: Mirror drawing: day 2
steps.do: Do today's five mirror-drawing tries (Experiment e2). Write down the time and the number of errors for each try. Ask: 'Is it easier than yesterday?'

steps.title: The brain hat
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Make a paper cap that fits your child's head. Draw the four lobes of the cortex on it: frontal at the forehead, parietal on top, temporal by the ears and occipital at the back. Hang a paper tail at the back of the neck for the cerebellum and the brainstem. Your child writes each part's main job on the hat as you explain it. Then talk about the two parts deep inside: the hippocampus and the amygdala.

steps.title: Two halves, and the people with split brains
steps.do: Say: 'The brain has two halves, called hemispheres. A thick bundle of nerves called the corpus callosum joins them. The left half controls the right side of the body, and the right half controls the left side. For most people, the left half does more of the work of language.' Then say: 'Epilepsy is an illness that causes seizures, sudden storms of electrical signals in the brain. In the 1960s, some people with very bad epilepsy had the corpus callosum cut, to stop seizures spreading. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga studied them. If a word was shown only to the right half, the person could not say it. But their left hand could pick out the matching object. Sometimes the talking half made up a reason for what the left hand did, without knowing it was making it up.' Ask: 'Was there one person inside, or two? Why might the brain make up explanations?' Let your child think. Don't settle it.

steps.title: The brain changes
steps.do: Say: 'Your brain is not fixed. Every time you learn, the connections between neurons change. This is called neuroplasticity. In 2000, Eleanor Maguire and her team scanned the brains of London taxi drivers, who spend years learning thousands of streets. The back part of their hippocampus, which helps us remember places, was larger than in other people. The longer they had driven, the larger it was.' Ask: 'Which part of your brain do you think is changing from what you practise?' (music, maths, a sport, a language). Say: 'Practising, getting it wrong and trying again is how the connections change.'

need: a large sheet of paper or an old cap, scissors, tape, markers

days.title: Three kinds of memory, and a man who lived in the present
days.goal: Learn the kinds of memory, meet Henry Molaison, and build a memory palace.

steps.title: Mirror drawing: day 3
steps.do: Do the last five mirror-drawing tries (Experiment e2). Then draw a graph: try number along the bottom, time up the side. Ask: 'When did it get easier? Do you remember how you did it, or do your hands just know?'

steps.title: Henry, Brenda and the mirror
steps.do: Tell voice v1. In 1953 a young man called Henry Molaison had parts of both sides of his brain removed, including most of the hippocampus, to stop his seizures. Afterwards he could not form new memories of events. Brenda Milner studied him and found he could still learn a skill: mirror drawing, the same thing you have been doing. He got better every day, yet each day he said he had never done it before. Ask the voice question. Then explain three kinds of memory: event memory ('my birthday last year'), fact memory ('Chennai is the capital of Tamil Nadu') and skill memory ('how to ride a cycle'). Ask your child to give one of each from their own life.

steps.title: A memory palace
steps.do: Do Activity a1, a memory palace. First read a plain list of ten other words once, and test it after 10 minutes. Then read the palace list once. Your child picks ten places along a walk they know well at home and puts each thing in a place with a funny picture. They walk the route in their mind and say the things in order. Test both lists again after 10 minutes and tomorrow.

steps.title: What if you couldn't make new memories?
steps.do: Ask: 'If, like Henry, you could not remember anything new, what would still be you?' (your skills, your old memories, your kindness, your laugh, your ways). Say: 'Henry helped scientists understand memory for over 50 years, but he could never remember doing it.' Ask: 'Should people like Henry be thanked in science books? How?' Your child writes one sentence they would want Henry to know.

days.title: Your memory is a storyteller
days.goal: Catch your memory inventing, and see why eyewitnesses can be honestly wrong.

steps.title: The word that was never said
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Ask first: 'Will you remember the words exactly? Will you add any that were not there?' Read the 15 words slowly, one each second. Count backwards from 60 together. Then your child writes every word they remember. Ask: 'Was the word "sleep" on the list?' Show the list. 'Sleep' was never read out.

steps.title: Smashed or hit?
steps.do: Tell voice v2. In 1974 Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed people a film of a car crash. They asked some people how fast the cars were going when they 'hit' each other. They asked others how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed into' each other. The 'smashed' group guessed higher speeds. A week later, more of them remembered broken glass, though there was none in the film. Ask the voice question. Say: 'Every time we remember, the brain rebuilds the memory from pieces, and new information can slip in. Scientists call this reconstructive memory. It does not mean people lie. It means a memory is not a recording.'

steps.title: Worksheet: the brain and memory (core)
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Your child explains each answer aloud. For the written items, ask them to give an example from their own life.

need: the word list from Experiment e1

days.title: Memory, history and attention
days.goal: Ask whose memories become history, and test what your brain does automatically.

steps.title: The story of one day, told three ways
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Your child asks three family members, one at a time, to tell the story of the same family event. Write each version in its own column, then compare them.

steps.title: Whose memories become history?
steps.do: Ask: 'If only one person's version of that day were written in a book, would it be the whole truth?' Say: 'History is memory written down. For most of the past, the people who could write, or who were powerful, chose what was kept. The memories of women, workers, enslaved people, tribal communities and children were often never written down. Today historians also record oral history: people's own spoken memories.' Ask: 'Whose memories in our family should we record before they are lost?' Plan to record one older relative's story this month.

steps.title: The Stroop test
steps.do: Do Experiment e3, the Stroop test. Ask first: 'Which card will be harder? Why?' Your child names the ink colour of each row on Card A, then the ink colour of each word on Card B. Time both cards and count the mistakes.

steps.title: Can you really multitask?
steps.do: Say: 'Reading is so practised that your brain did it automatically, even when you did not want to. Attention cannot really do two hard things at once. It switches quickly between them, and each switch costs time and causes mistakes.' Ask: 'What happens to homework with a phone buzzing next to it?'

need: three family members (in person or on the phone)
red, blue, green and black pens, and paper for the Stroop cards

days.title: Why do we sleep?
days.goal: Learn what happens in sleep and meet a live debate.

steps.title: A night of sleep
steps.do: Draw a 'night graph' with your child, from falling asleep to waking. Say: 'All night, the brain goes round in cycles of about 90 minutes. First comes light sleep. Then deep sleep, with slow brain waves, when the body repairs itself and makes growth hormone. Then REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement: the eyes dart under the lids, the brain is very active and the most vivid dreams happen. Then round again. There is more deep sleep early in the night and more REM near morning.' Ask: 'Why might waking from REM sleep help you remember a dream?' (you were in the middle of it). Say: 'In deep sleep, the hippocampus replays the day's events. Scientists have recorded this replay in rats who had run mazes. Many think it helps move memories into long-term storage in the cortex.'

steps.title: Washing the brain at night?
steps.do: Tell voice v4. In 2013 Maiken Nedergaard's team reported that in sleeping mice, fluid flows through the brain much faster and washes out waste. In 2024 a team led by Nicholas Franks and William Wisden found the opposite in their mice. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Strange sleepers
steps.do: Say: 'Dolphins can sleep with one half of the brain at a time. They keep one eye open and keep swimming up to breathe. Some birds do this too. Frigatebirds have been recorded sleeping in short bursts while flying over the sea. Every animal studied so far seems to need some kind of sleep or rest, even fruit flies and jellyfish.' Ask: 'Sleep is dangerous for wild animals. So why do they all still sleep?' (sleep must do something too important to lose).

steps.title: Worksheet: apply it (stretch)
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Let your child use the night graph and the results of e1, e2 and e3.

days.title: Feelings and consciousness
days.goal: Compare two views of emotions, ask which animals are conscious, and face the hardest question.

steps.title: Emotion charades
steps.do: Each player acts an emotion with face and body only, no words: joy, fear, anger, disgust, surprise, sadness, then harder ones: jealousy, pride, embarrassment, relief, nostalgia. Others guess. Ask: 'Which were easy to guess? Which were hard? Would someone from a very different culture guess the same?'

steps.title: Are emotions built in or built?
steps.do: Tell voice v3. Paul Ekman argued that there are a few basic emotions, each with a face that people everywhere recognise. Lisa Feldman Barrett argues that the brain builds each emotion from body feelings, past experience and culture. Ask the voice question. Then ask: 'In charades, which emotions did everyone guess? Does that help Ekman's side or Barrett's?'

steps.title: Who else is conscious?
steps.do: Say: 'In 1970 Gordon Gallup gave chimpanzees a medicine that put them into a deep sleep, then put a red mark on their faces. When they woke and saw themselves in a mirror, they touched the mark on their own faces. This is called the mirror test. Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies have passed versions of it. In 2019 scientists reported that a small fish, the cleaner wrasse, seemed to pass it too, and others argued about what that means. Dogs know the world mostly by smell, so a mirror may be the wrong test for them.' Then say: 'In 2024 a group of scientists signed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. It says there is strong evidence that mammals and birds have conscious experience. It says there is a realistic possibility that all animals with backbones, and many others such as octopuses and bees, have it too.' Ask: 'Bees feel things in their own way. Does that change how we should treat them?'

steps.title: What is consciousness?
steps.do: Say: 'Being aware, having a "what it is like" to be you, is called consciousness. How a brain gives rise to it is the biggest open question in science.' Then say: 'Here is where we start from. Everything is aware in its own way, from a single cell to a person. A brain is one way awareness shows up, not the only way. Remember the slime mould from Class 3, who found the shortest way through a maze with no brain at all.' Then lay out three other views, each on a card. 1. Emergence: most neuroscientists think consciousness appears when enough neurons work together, the way a traffic jam appears from many cars, though no single car is a jam. 2. Panpsychism: some philosophers say a simple form of experience is part of everything, and brains combine it. 3. The philosopher Daniel Dennett said consciousness is less mysterious than it feels, and is just what brains do. Ask: 'Which view seems most likely to you? What evidence would change your mind? Could a computer that talks like a person be conscious?' Then your child draws a self-portrait: their face, and inside it, whatever they think they really are.

need: paper and cards for the views

days.title: Mind or Myth: game, challenge and teach it back
days.goal: Put it all together and teach it back.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3, the challenge sheet. The written answers matter most. Let your child argue both sides out loud before writing.

steps.title: Mind or Myth?
steps.do: Play the card game g1. For each card, the player says 'mind fact', 'myth' or 'still argued', and why.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child wears the brain hat and teaches a family member the main parts, then runs the false-memory word test on them (e1) and explains what happened. Ask the check questions. Ask what changed in how they think about their own memory.

sections.p: Match each part to its main job.
The left half of the brain mostly controls…
opts: the left side of the body
the right side of the body

sections.p: The brain's ability to change its connections as we learn is called neuro____ .
Eleanor Maguire, a brain scientist, scanned the brains of London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets. Which part of the brain was larger in them?
Which kind of memory?

your last birthday
Chennai is the capital of Tamil Nadu
tying shoelaces
the day you lost a tooth

sections.p: Henry Molaison could not form new event memories, but he could…
opts: remember what he had for lunch

sections.p: In the word test, many people 'remembered' the word 'sleep', though it was never read out. Why?
opts: the brain keeps the main idea and rebuilds the details
the word was hidden inside another word

sections.p: Two honest people remember the same day differently. How can both be telling the truth as they remember it?
Why might an eyewitness in a courtroom be wrong without lying?
Your mirror drawing got faster each day. Which kind of memory was that?
In the Stroop test, it took longer to name the ink colour of colour words than of XXXX rows. Why?
opts: reading is so automatic it gets in the way

sections.p: Light sleep, deep sleep or REM?
items: eyes darting under the lids
slow brain waves and body repair
most vivid dreams
easy to wake
more of it early in the night

sections.p: Dolphins can sleep with one ____ of the brain at a time.
Multitasking is really…
opts: doing two hard things at once perfectly
switching attention quickly, with a cost

sections.p: Your family told one event three ways. Which version should go in the family history? Or should all three? Why?

Two teams studied sleeping mice. Maiken Nedergaard's team found that fluid washes through the brain faster during sleep. Nicholas Franks's team found it was slower. How could scientists find out which is right?
Match the scientist to the finding.
pairs: Henry Molaison learned mirror drawing without remembering learning it
the words in a question can change a memory
taxi drivers' brains changed with learning
chimpanzees recognise themselves in a mirror

sections.p: Settled or still argued?
items: the hippocampus is needed to form new event memories
memories are rebuilt each time
exactly why we sleep
whether emotions are built in or built by each brain
how much bees feel, and what it is like to be a bee
the brain changes as we learn

sections.p: In a split-brain patient, the two halves of the brain are no longer joined. The talking half made up a reason for what the left hand did. What does that suggest?
opts: the brain can make up explanations without knowing it
the left hand was moving by itself

sections.p: Which is the best reason the mirror test may be unfair to dogs?
opts: dogs rely more on smell than sight

sections.p: Myth or supported by evidence?
items: people learn best only in their own 'learning style'
we use only 10% of our brain
sleep helps memory
practice changes the brain
listening to Mozart makes babies cleverer

sections.p: Because the brain rebuilds memories, we can imagine and plan. But it also means our memories can be wrong. Is a rebuilt memory more of a help or a problem? Argue both sides.
Which view of consciousness do you find most convincing, and what evidence would change your mind?
Could a computer program that talks like a person be conscious? How could anyone tell?
Bees and octopuses feel things in their own way. What should change in how people treat them?

experiments.title: The word that was never said
experiments.question: Does memory record what happened, or rebuild it?
steps: Tell your child: 'I'll read some words. Listen carefully. Afterwards, write down as many as you can.'
Read slowly, one word a second: bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, wake, snooze, blanket, doze, slumber, snore, nap, peace, yawn, drowsy.
Wait 1 minute (count backwards from 60 together), then your child writes every word they remember.
Ask: 'Are you sure every word you wrote was on the list?' Then ask: 'Was the word "sleep" on the list?'
Show the list. 'Sleep' was never said. Try it on other family members.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will you remember the words exactly? Will you add any that weren't there?'
experiments.observe: Many people, children and adults, write or confidently 'remember' the word 'sleep', which was never read out.
experiments.why: This is the Deese–Roediger–McDermott test, published by Henry Roediger and Kathleen McDermott in 1995, building on James Deese's work in 1959. The brain doesn't store each word separately. It stores the main idea, called the gist ('words about sleep'), and rebuilds the details when you recall. The gist suggests 'sleep', so memory adds it, and it can feel just as real as the true words. The same rebuilding lets us plan and imagine.

experiments.title: Mirror drawing
experiments.question: Can you learn a skill without remembering learning it?
need: a mirror that can stand up (a dressing-table mirror, or a hand mirror propped against a wall)
a book or card held above the drawing hand, so your child cannot see the hand directly
15 copies of a star drawn with a double outline (two lines about 5 mm apart), drawn or photocopied
steps: Stand the mirror upright behind the paper. Hold the book above your child's hand, so they can see the paper only in the mirror.
Your child traces around the star between the two lines, looking only in the mirror.
Time each try and count how many times the pencil goes outside the lines.
Five tries on Day 1, five on Day 2, five on Day 3. Record all times and errors.
On Day 3 draw a graph: try number along the bottom, time up the side.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'How hard will it be? Will you get better? How fast?'
experiments.observe: The first tries are slow and wobbly, with many errors. Most children get much faster and more accurate over the three days, sometimes with a jump after a night's sleep.
experiments.why: Brenda Milner gave this test to Henry Molaison in the early 1960s. Henry improved over days like you did, though he never remembered doing it before. It showed that skill memory uses different parts of the brain (including the cerebellum and deep areas called the basal ganglia) from event memory, which needs the hippocampus. Your hands learn the skill before you can explain how.
experiments.safety: No safety concerns. Use a mirror with smooth edges, or one in a frame.

experiments.title: The Stroop test
experiments.question: Can your brain stop itself from reading?
need: red, blue, green and black pens
steps: Card A: write 20 rows of XXXX in red, blue, green and black, mixed up.
Card B: write 20 colour words, each written in a DIFFERENT colour ink from what it says (the word 'red' written in blue ink, and so on).
Your child names the INK colour of each row of Card A, as fast as possible. Time it.
Then names the INK colour (not the word) of each word on Card B. Time it and count mistakes.
Try it on a younger child who can't read yet, if you can.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which card will be harder? Why?'
experiments.observe: Card B takes longer and causes more mistakes. Readers often say the word instead of the colour. Children who cannot read yet find both cards about equally easy.
experiments.why: John Ridley Stroop described this in 1935. Reading is so practised that the brain does it automatically, even when you're trying to name the colour. Your attention has to fight the automatic habit, and that takes time. Much of what the brain does happens without our choosing. Practice turns slow, careful skills into fast, automatic ones.

activities.title: A memory palace
need: the palace list below, and a plain list of 10 other words (for example: pen, river, cup, horse, cloud, spoon, drum, leaf, key, boat)
steps: Read the plain list once and test it after 10 minutes. Then read this palace list once: onions, ladder, umbrella, coconut, toothbrush, kite, bangles, a goat, glue, a drum.
Your child chooses a walk they know very well, like from the front door to their bed, and picks 10 places along it (the door, the shoe rack, the sofa, the fridge…).
Put each thing in a place with a funny, clear picture: onions piled on the doormat, making the door cry. A ladder lying across the shoe rack. An umbrella opening inside the fridge.
Your child walks the route in their mind and says each item.
Test the palace list after 10 minutes and again tomorrow. Test the plain list tomorrow too, and compare.
Tell your child: speakers in ancient Greece and Rome used this method, and memory champions still use it.
activities.outcome: Your child can remember 10 things in order using places, and sees that linking new things to a route they know well makes them easier to remember.

activities.title: One day, told three ways
steps: Choose a family event that several people were at: a wedding, a trip, a festival, a power cut.
Your child asks each person separately (in person or on the phone): 'What happened? Who was there? What was the weather? What did you eat? What was the funniest or most important moment?'
Write each answer in its own column.
Circle what everyone agrees on and underline what they disagree on.
Ask: 'Who do you think is right about the disagreements? Is there a photo or video to check? Does a photo show everything?'
activities.outcome: Three versions of one day, and an understanding that memories differ honestly and history needs many voices.

activities.title: The brain hat
need: a large sheet of paper or an old cap
steps: Make a paper cap that fits your child's head (a strip round the head and two strips crossing over the top).

Draw the lobes of the cortex on it: frontal at the forehead (planning, choosing, controlling yourself), parietal on top (touch and knowing where your body is), temporal by the ears (hearing, language and memory), occipital at the back (seeing).
On a tail of paper hanging at the back of the neck, draw the cerebellum (balance and skilled movement) and the brainstem (breathing, heartbeat, waking and sleeping).
Explain that deep inside, where we can't draw on a hat, are the hippocampus (making new event memories) and the amygdala (alarm and fear).
Say: 'These are main jobs, not the whole story. Almost everything you do uses many parts working together.'
activities.outcome: A wearable map of the brain your child made and can teach from.

project.title: My mind lab notebook
steps: Record your mirror-drawing times and errors (Days 1–3) and draw the graph.
Record your memory palace results and the plain-list results (Day 3–4).
Record the false-memory test on yourself and on two family members (Day 4).
Record the Stroop times and mistakes (Day 5).
Write the three versions of one family day (Day 5).
On Day 8, write one page: 'What I found out about my own mind', with your best graph and one question you still have.
project.outcome: A notebook of real experiments on your own mind, with graphs and a question to keep exploring.

game.title: Mind or Myth?
rules: On your turn, read a card aloud and say: 'mind fact', 'myth' or 'still argued'.
Turn it over. Right, with a good reason: keep the card. For 'still argued' cards, you keep it if you can give one argument on each side.
Anyone can challenge an answer by giving evidence. The group decides.

cards.front: We only use 10% of our brain.
cards.back: Myth: scans show activity all over the brain.

cards.front: Memories are rebuilt each time we remember.
People learn best when teaching matches their 'learning style'.
cards.back: Myth: careful tests haven't found this.

cards.front: Exactly why we need to sleep.
cards.back: Still argued: memory, repair and brain-cleaning ideas are all debated.

cards.front: The hippocampus is needed to form new event memories.
Listening to Mozart makes children cleverer.
cards.back: Myth: the 1993 'Mozart effect' was small, short and often didn't repeat.

cards.front: London taxi drivers' brains changed with learning.
Emotions are built in, with the same faces everywhere.
Dolphins can sleep with half their brain.
A fish can pass the mirror test.
Some people are left-brained and some are right-brained.
cards.back: Myth: both halves work together in everyone.
Mind fact: each switch costs time.

cards.front: An eyewitness who is sure must be right.
cards.back: Myth: confident memories can still be wrong.

cards.front: Whether a computer can be conscious.
Skills can be learned without remembering learning them.
Bees can learn and seem to play.
cards.back: Mind fact: bumblebees learn to roll a small ball for a reward, and some roll balls even with no reward. How much bees feel is still being studied.

cards.front: Consciousness is made only by brains.
cards.back: Still argued: most neuroscientists think so. The slime mould solves mazes with no brain, and some philosophers say awareness is part of everything.

voices.who: Brenda Milner (born 1918), Britain and Canada, and Henry Molaison (1926–2008), USA
voices.idea: In 1953 Henry Molaison, a young man with severe epilepsy, had surgery that removed parts of both sides of his brain, including most of the hippocampus. His seizures improved, but he could no longer form new memories of events: he would meet someone, and minutes later not know them. Brenda Milner, a psychologist in Montreal, studied him from 1955. She showed that he could still learn a skill, mirror drawing, getting better day after day while never remembering having done it.
voices.then: Many scientists then thought memory was spread evenly through the brain. Milner's work showed that a particular part, the hippocampus, is needed to form new event memories, and that skill memory works separately.
voices.now: Her findings are the foundation of memory science, and she kept working past the age of 100. Henry was known for decades only as 'H.M.', to protect his privacy, and was studied by over 100 scientists. His name was revealed after his death in 2008. He is now seen as one of the most important people in the history of brain science, though he never knew it.
voices.ask: Henry gave science more than almost anyone, but never chose to and never knew. How should science thank people like him?

voices.idea: In 1974, with John Palmer, Loftus showed people a film of a car crash. She asked how fast the cars were going when they 'hit' or 'smashed into' each other. The 'smashed' group guessed higher speeds. A week later they were more likely to remember broken glass that was not in the film. In later studies, her team found that some people could be led to 'remember' whole childhood events that never happened, such as being lost in a shopping mall.
voices.then: Her work was controversial, especially when she gave evidence in court that witnesses' memories could be wrong. Some people felt she cast doubt on real victims.
voices.now: That memory is reconstructive and can be changed by questions is well accepted, and it has changed how police in many countries question witnesses. How often whole false memories can be created, and how far her lab results apply to real life, are still debated.
voices.ask: If memories can change, should a court ever convict someone on one eyewitness alone? What else would you want?

voices.who: Paul Ekman (born 1934), USA, and Lisa Feldman Barrett (born 1963), USA: what are emotions?
voices.idea: From the 1960s, Ekman showed photos of faces to people in many countries, including a remote group in Papua New Guinea. Many matched the faces to the same emotions. He argued that a few basic emotions, such as happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust, are built into all humans. Barrett argues instead that the brain builds each emotion, each time, from body feelings, the situation, past experience, and the words and culture we've learned. She points out that the same emotion can look very different in different people.
voices.then: Ekman's view became the standard one and is used in many textbooks and computer programs that try to read faces.
voices.now: Scientists still disagree. Studies show faces are recognised above chance across cultures, but much less reliably than once thought, and that context changes how we read a face. Many researchers now take a middle view. Programs that claim to read emotions from faces are widely criticised.
voices.ask: If emotions are built from body feelings plus words, could learning more emotion words change how you feel?

voices.who: Maiken Nedergaard, Denmark and USA, and Nicholas Franks, Britain: does sleep wash the brain?
voices.idea: In 2013, Nedergaard's team reported that in sleeping mice the spaces between brain cells widen and fluid flows through much faster, washing away waste, including a protein linked to Alzheimer's disease. They called it the glymphatic system. The idea that sleep 'cleans the brain' became very popular.
voices.then: Many scientists were excited. Some questioned the methods, such as the use of anaesthesia and dyes.
voices.now: In 2024, a team led by Nicholas Franks and William Wisden reported in their experiments with mice that clearance of a dye from the brain was actually lower during sleep and anaesthesia. Both teams stand by their results. Whether, and how much, sleep cleans the human brain is now a live debate, and why we sleep is still not fully known.
voices.ask: Two careful teams found opposite results with mice. What would you need to know about each experiment to decide whom to believe?

story.title: What the Handycam Saw
text: I am a video camera, a small silver Handycam. I live in a shoebox on the top shelf of a cupboard in a flat in Kochi, under three folded blankets and a bag of old school certificates. Nobody has switched me on for eight years, and my battery is dead. But on the little memory card inside me, I still have everything I ever saw.

I saw a lot of weddings. That was my main job. Devika's mother bought me when Devika was born. I was there at Devika's first rice-feeding, the choroonu, and at every birthday and every wedding in the family. I saw a great many banana leaves full of food and a great many uncles dancing badly.
Last Onam, the cousins came. Devika is eleven now, and her cousin Anju is ten. They had not seen each other for a year. They sat on the floor eating banana chips and arguing.
"I didn't fall in," said Anju. "You fell in."

"I did not!" said Devika. "You fell in the kulam at Remya Chechi's wedding. I remember it exactly. You were wearing a yellow frock. You were trying to catch a duck, and you slipped on the steps, and splash! Everyone came running. Your frock was all green with weeds."

Anju's face went red. "That's not what happened. I remember it. You were trying to catch the duck. You were wearing that green silk pavadai. You slipped and went in up to your neck, and Ammavan pulled you out, and you cried and cried."
"I never cry."
"You cried so much they gave you three helpings of payasam."
They were both sure. I could hear it in their voices. Neither of them was lying. Each of them could see it, the pond and the steps and the duck and the splash, as clearly as I could have shown it.
"Ask Amma," said Devika.
Devika's mother was frying pappadams in the kitchen. She said, "Oh, that wedding! Somebody fell in, I remember that. I think it was one of you. Or was it Chinnu? Wait, I filmed everything."
And that is how, after eight years, I was taken down from the cupboard.

It took a whole evening to find a charger and a cable and an old television that would take me. The whole family crowded round: the cousins, the parents, Ammavan and the girl from next door. Devika's mother pressed play, and there it was: Remya Chechi's wedding, 2016, at the old family house near Alappuzha. There was a pandal of woven coconut leaves, and at the end of the garden a green kulam, a pond with stone steps going down into it. I had been pointed at the kulam for most of the afternoon, because there were ducks and the light was nice.

There were the ducks. There was a little girl in a yellow frock, Anju, about two years old, toddling on the bank with a piece of banana. There was another little girl in a green silk pavadai, Devika, about three, holding her mother's hand. Nobody fell in.
"Wait," said Devika. "Fast forward."

We watched the whole afternoon. The ducks. The steps. The pandal. A long, boring piece where I was pointed at the ground because somebody forgot to switch me off. And then, near sunset, a man came down the steps to wash his hands. He slipped on the green weed, waved his arms like a windmill, and sat down in the kulam with an enormous splash. Everyone ran. Somebody pulled him out. He was laughing and dripping, with weeds on his head.
It was Ammavan.
The room went completely silent. Then Ammavan, who was sitting on the sofa with his tea, began to laugh so hard that he spilled it.

"I'd forgotten!" he said. "I'd completely forgotten! I told that story at every family function for years. 'Remember when I fell in the kulam?' I used to say to the children. 'You were there, you saw it!'"
Anju and Devika looked at each other.
"But I remember it," said Anju, slowly. "I remember the duck. I remember the cold water."
"So do I," said Devika. "I can see it."

And they could. That is the strange thing. They had heard the story so many times, at so many family functions, that their brains had taken the pieces, the kulam, the duck, the steps, the splash, and built a memory out of them. Each of them, without knowing, had put a child into it: herself, or the other one. Every time they remembered it, they built it again, and every time it felt more real.
Anju was quiet for a while. Then she said, "Is anything I remember real?"
Devika's mother switched me off. She thought about it.
"Most of it, probably," she said. "The important parts. But a memory is not a video. Your brain builds it again each time you remember. So hold your memories a little loosely."
"And the camera?" said Devika. "The camera's always right."

I would like to say yes. I would like to be the one who knows the truth. But I only saw what I was pointed at. I didn't see the kitchen, or the dancing, or what anybody was thinking. Half the wedding happened behind me. If somebody had fallen in on the other side of the garden, I would never have known.
They put me back in my shoebox that night, but not on the top shelf. Anju asked if she could keep me in her bag till the end of the holidays.

I think she wanted to film something. I think she wanted to remember it properly this time, and then I think she understood that she would have to remember it anyway, the way everyone does: a little bit right, a little bit wrong, and her own.
story.epiphany: Each time we remember, the brain rebuilds the event from pieces. A story heard many times can become a memory that feels completely real, with ourselves placed inside it. The turn is the video showing Ammavan, not either girl, falling in. A second turn questions the evidence too: the camera only saw what it was pointed at.
ask: Why were both Anju and Devika so sure?
Was either of them lying? How can you be honest and wrong at the same time?
Where did their memories come from?
The camera says it 'only saw what I was pointed at'. Why does that matter?
Is there a family story you 'remember' that you might only have heard?

ideas.idea: A memory is rebuilt each time, not played back like a recording.
ideas.more: Each time we recall something, the brain rebuilds it from pieces, and new information can slip in. The false-memory word test and the family-story activity show this. The same rebuilding lets us imagine and plan.

ideas.idea: Much of the mind runs without us.
ideas.more: Reflexes, the Stroop effect, skills learned without remembering, and the reasons made up by split-brain patients all show that much happens below awareness. Ask: who is 'you', then?

ideas.idea: Consciousness is the biggest open question.
ideas.more: Everything is aware in its own way, and nobody knows how a brain gives rise to our kind of experience, what it is like to be another being, or whether a machine could be aware. Emergence, panpsychism and other views are all still argued. A child today could one day help answer it.

unknowns: What is consciousness, and how does a brain (or anything) produce experience? Nobody knows.
Why do we need sleep? Memory, repair and brain-cleaning ideas all have evidence, and the cleaning idea is now hotly debated.
What is it like to be a bee or an octopus? The 2024 New York Declaration says many animals may have conscious experience, but no test lets us feel it from the inside.
big: If memories are rebuilt every time, is your past real?
Are you the one thinking your thoughts, or the one watching them?
Could consciousness exist without a brain, or without matter at all?
If a robot said it felt sad, should we believe it?
Whose memories become history, and who decides?

challenge.q: 'Everyone has a learning style (visual, auditory or kinaesthetic), and teaching should match it.'
challenge.hint: Many people prefer certain ways of learning, but when scientists (for example Harold Pashler and colleagues, 2008) looked for careful tests showing that matching teaching to a style improves learning, they found almost no good evidence. What helps most people: spaced practice, testing yourself, connecting to what you know, and using several senses together. Ask: why might a popular idea spread without evidence?

challenge.q: 'I'm sure of it, so it must be true.'
challenge.hint: Confidence and accuracy are not the same. The false-memory test and the Loftus studies show people can be completely sure of things that never happened. Ask: what can you do when you feel sure?

challenge.q: 'Humans have the most advanced mind of all animals because our brains are special.'
challenge.hint: Our brains have many neurons in the cortex for our size, and we use language and build cultures. But crows, octopuses and bees solve problems with very different brains, and a slime mould with none. Suzana Herculano-Houzel, a Brazilian brain scientist, counted the neurons in many brains. She found that ours is a scaled-up primate brain, not a different kind. Ask: is one kind of mind the best, or is each mind good at what that animal's life needs?

perspectives.view: As a graduate student in 1973, Pert designed and carried out the experiment that found the opiate receptor. This is a molecule in the brain that painkilling chemicals fit into, like a key in a lock. In 1978 a major prize for the work went to her supervisor and others, not to her, and she protested publicly. Ask: who should get credit, the person with the plan, the one who does the work, or both?

perspectives.who: A storyteller in an oral tradition
perspectives.view: Before writing, and still today in many communities, epics, family histories and songs are carried in memory and passed on aloud. In southern Tamil Nadu, villu paattu singers tell long stories to the beat of a giant bow-shaped instrument. Rhythm, music and place help them remember. Ask: what does an oral tradition keep that a book might lose, and what might change each time it's told?
A dolphin sleeps one half of their brain at a time, so that they can keep swimming and come up to breathe. Ask: what would it be like never to be fully asleep?

books.title: Your Fantastic Elastic Brain: Stretch It, Shape It
books.author: JoAnn Deak
books.why: A gentle recap of neuroplasticity and learning from mistakes.

books.title: Moonwalking with Einstein
books.author: Joshua Foer
books.why: A journalist trains his memory with memory palaces and goes on to win a national memory contest.

books.title: The Seven Sins of Memory
books.author: Daniel L. Schacter
books.why: How and why memory goes wrong, by a leading memory scientist.

books.title: Are We Smart Enough to Know How Smart Animals Are?
books.author: Frans de Waal
books.why: A primatologist on animal minds, mirror tests and how we test other species unfairly.

check.q: Name four parts of the brain and their main jobs.
check.a: For example: brainstem, breathing and heartbeat. Cerebellum, balance and skilled movement. Hippocampus, new event memories. Cortex, thinking, sensing and planning. Amygdala, alarm and fear.

check.q: What did Henry Molaison's story teach scientists?
check.a: The hippocampus is needed to form new event memories, and skill memory works separately.

check.q: What happened in the false-memory word test, and why?
check.a: Many people 'remembered' the word 'sleep', which was never read out. Memory keeps the main idea and rebuilds the details.

check.q: Why might an honest eyewitness be wrong?
check.a: Memory is rebuilt each time we recall it, so questions and later information can change it.

check.q: What happens during a night's sleep?
check.a: Cycles of light, deep and REM sleep. Deep sleep is for repair and replaying memories. REM sleep has the most vivid dreams.

check.q: What are the two views of emotions?
check.a: Ekman says a few basic emotions are built in. Feldman Barrett says the brain builds each emotion from body feelings, the situation and culture.

check.q: Give two views of what consciousness is, and say which you find most convincing.
check.a: For example: consciousness emerges from many neurons working together, or experience is part of everything. Then the child's own view, with a reason.

check.q: Is a strong feeling of being sure enough to know a memory is true?
check.a: No. Confident memories can be wrong, so check with other evidence.
